actions.justification: MANDATORY - deadline 10 minutes. Patient has critical vitals: SpO2 85%, RR 30, HR 108, temp 38.1°C. Immediate vital signs assessment required per GOLD COPD guideline.
MANDATORY - Patient has severe respiratory compromise with SpO2 85%, RR 30, severe dyspnea and wheezing. Respiratory status assessment is critical to guide treatment intensity and NIV eligibility.

MANDATORY per GOLD COPD guideline for severe exacerbation. ABG is essential to assess degree of hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis to guide oxygen therapy and determine need for ventilatory support.
MANDATORY action per scenario requirements. Chest X-ray is required in COPD exacerbation assessment to identify precipitants (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema) and guide treatment decisions.

GOLD guideline mandates bronchodilator within 30 minutes for severe COPD exacerbation. Patient is at 15 minutes with critical SpO2 85% and RR 30 - must not delay further. Short-acting beta-agonist and anticholinergic nebulization indicated.

SpO2 is critically low at 85%. Controlled supplemental oxygen is needed to target SpO2 88-92% in COPD patients (avoiding hypercapnic drive suppression). High-flow O2 without monitoring is contraindicated per guidelines.
Mandatory per GOLD COPD guidelines for severe exacerbation. Reduces airway inflammation and improves outcomes. Not yet administered.
Mandatory per GOLD COPD guidelines for severe exacerbation, especially with purulent sputum indicating likely bacterial infection. Patient has fever (38.1°C) supporting infectious etiology.
Mandatory per GOLD COPD guidelines. Patient has SpO2 85%, RR 30, and severe dyspnea — strong candidate for non-invasive ventilation. Must assess eligibility before initiating NIV.

Patient has severe hypoxia (SpO2 85%) and tachycardia with RR 30 - mental status assessment is critical to evaluate for CO2 narcosis or altered consciousness which would affect NIV eligibility and urgency of intubation.

Patient has CKD stage 3b and diabetes - BMP is essential to assess renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and bicarbonate (to evaluate metabolic compensation in the setting of respiratory acidosis from COPD exacerbation with decreased urine output).

Patient has fever (38.1°C) and purulent sputum suggesting infectious exacerbation - CBC will assess for leukocytosis, neutrophilia, or signs of hematologic compromise contributing to the exacerbation.
Patient has purulent sputum suggesting bacterial infection. Sputum culture will guide antibiotic therapy, especially important given CKD stage 3b which limits antibiotic choices and dosing.
Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral etiology in COPD exacerbation, guiding antibiotic stewardship. Elevated levels support continuation of antibiotics already initiated.
Patient has fever (38.1°C), tachycardia (HR 108), and severe exacerbation — blood cultures should be obtained to rule out bacteremia/sepsis before empiric antibiotics take full effect.

Patient has tachycardia, elevated RR, decreased urine output, and SpO2 of 85% — lactate helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion/sepsis as a complicating factor in this severe COPD exacerbation with infectious trigger.

Severe COPD exacerbation with SpO2 85%, RR 30, and multiple comorbidities (CKD 3b, DM2, GOLD stage 3) warrants pulmonology involvement for NIV management decisions and advanced respiratory support planning.

Purulent sputum with worsening dyspnea and persistent hypoxia despite initial treatment — CT chest can identify complications such as pneumonia consolidation, pulmonary embolism, or pneumothorax not visible on plain film.

Patient has decreased urine output, elevated BP (150/90), and CKD stage 3b. While cautious use is warranted given CKD, the clinical picture with hypertension and reduced urine output suggests possible fluid retention contributing to respiratory compromise. A cautious dose of diuretic may help reduce preload and improve dyspnea, monitoring renal function closely.

Patient has decreased urine output and CKD stage 3b; cautious IV fluid administration may help maintain renal perfusion. However, given the severe dyspnea and possible fluid overload risk, this should be titrated carefully. All mandatory COPD exacerbation actions are already completed.

Patient has elevated MAP of 110 with HR 108, however this is the only available action remaining. Given the patient's severe COPD exacerbation with SpO2 85%, leukocytosis, and all mandatory treatments already completed, vasopressor use is not typically indicated here but is the only available action in this phase. Monitoring hemodynamic status is appropriate given the clinical severity and comorbidities (CKD 3b, diabetes). Note: vasopressors are generally not first-line for COPD exacerbation; this selection is made as it is the sole remaining available action in the current phase.

NIV eligibility has been assessed. Given persistent severe hypoxemia (SpO2 85%), RR 30, and severe COPD exacerbation, initiating non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) is strongly indicated per GOLD guidelines to reduce work of breathing and improve oxygenation. Sedatives are contraindicated, making NIV the preferred ventilatory support.

Patient has CKD stage 3b with decreased urine output. Diuretics and IV fluids have been given, and antibiotics (potentially nephrotoxic) are being administered. Serial monitoring of renal function and urine output is critical to avoid AKI.

Patient has Type 2 diabetes and is receiving systemic corticosteroids, which commonly cause hyperglycemia. Blood glucose monitoring is essential to detect and manage steroid-induced hyperglycemia and prevent diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar states.
